DESIGN 1: Design 1 is an introductory course that will explore the fundamental skills, methods, and mindsets of human-centered design. This course is intended for any student who is curious about the design major or wants to learn more about design. It is a required course for all design majors, and provides foundational understanding for subsequent coursework. This course is highly experiential and collaborative. We will cover core design methods through project-based learning and incorporate real world challenges. Students will experience how to prototype and test concepts, research needs, and how to synthesize insights from data to spark novel ideas. Each project will illuminate how design methods can be used to create positive impact in the world. The course will also help students understand possible career pathways for designers through an inspiring and diverse set of guest speakers and project leads.
DESIGN 11: Visual Thinking is a foundational class for all designers and makers at Stanford. Through a series of projects, you learn how to bring your creativity to life. Visual thinking, a powerful adjunct to other problem solving modalities, is developed and exercised in the context of design challenges. Through projects you expand access to your imagination, see more clearly with the "mind's eye", and learn how to do rapid visualization and prototyping. You will advance your skills in building in the physical and digital world while strengthening your ability to generate and refine ideas.
DESIGN 44N: What does it mean to design with life? In this seminar, we'll make as much as possible with as much as possible of a single tree in an attempt to find out. The quarter is a collective experimental process and design challenge: working together, how much of this material can we transform into "useful" artifacts, and what do those transformations reveal? We'll explore across scales, from the micro to the macro. And experiment with and develop processes, tools, and methods such as milling, handtools, joinery, papermaking, printing, natural dyes, biochar, fibers, and substrates for next-generation bio-based materials. This hands-on investigation allows us to explore fundamental questions. Where are the real limits of "circularity"? How does structure create properties? How might natural selection and biological evolution inspire and constrain design and the creative process? What kinds of new knowledge and innovative ideas can be generated through making? What might a more-than-human-centered design process look like? By investigating the relationship between the biological and the material, we'll cultivate curious, experimental, and prototyping mindsets that are foundational skills to both biology and design. By building bridges between biology and design, we will find insights and opportunities in interdisciplinarity to understand and create in new ways. Class sessions mix field visits, hands-on work, labs, and structured documentation and reflection. By quarter's end, you'll contribute to a body of experimental processes for local, small-scale material craft and manufacturing and to a collective exhibition tracing our tree's many possible futures. You'll leave with foundational skills in fabrication and material inquiry, experience in embodied research, bio-based materials, and an orientation to advanced scientific and creative research. No background in biology, craft, or design required. Just curiosity and a commitment to learning through doing.
DESIGN 60: A hands-on exploration of the elements and principles of design common to all the visual arts. Through a mix of theory, analysis, and practice the student will develop their ability to interpret visual content and produce effective imagery.
DESIGN 101: This course explores the interconnections between the history and ethics of design. The guiding framework of our exploration emphasizes that designers both reflect and shape history, and that all of design has a set of values that influences the design process and how the end products of that process are used. Since these values are embedded in larger (often socially inherited) sets of values, this course introduces prominent ethical frameworks. The course highlights the key advantages and challenges of each theory, the ways in which they shape a designer's ethos, and how they influence our conceptions of harm and justifiable value tradeoffs. The course emphasizes ethical reasoning as a foundational design skill, guiding students to (i) evaluate competing ethical perspectives on human problems, (ii) adapt and apply theoretical principles and concepts specifically in the domain of design, and (iii) to defend their ethical judgments about design choices using moral theories and frameworks. The course also explores key moments in the history of design which allow for practical applications of these moral frameworks. This class will ask you to read, write, and produce several alternative forms of media in order to research and explore both ethical and historical topics. This course is required for undergraduate students in the Design Major and, as such, priority will be given to these students; higher priority to juniors and seniors. If you are not in the Design program, instructor permission based on application is needed for enrollment.
DESIGN 121: An intensive project-based class that introduces the central philosophy of the product design program. Students learn how to use the lens of human needs to innovate at the intersection of technical factors (feasibility), business factors (viability), and human values (desirability). Students work toward mastery of the human-centered design methodology through several real-world, team-based projects. Students gain fluency in designing solutions ranging from physical products, to digital interfaces, to services and experiences. Students are immersed in building their individual and team capacities around core design process and methods, and emerge with a strong foundation in needfinding, synthesis, ideation, rapid prototyping, user testing, iteration, and storytelling. This class is required for undergrad Design majors. This class is for Design students only.
DESIGN 131: Needfinding focuses on design research and design planning. The premise of the class is that by studying the world around us, we can get a better understanding of what people need, and use those insights to create meaningful new products and services. Needfinding draws upon theory and methods from anthropology, psychology, engineering and design planning. In this class, students develop proficiency in research and planning through a combination of in- class activities, readings on theory and real world projects. Emphasis is on developing the flexible thinking skills that enable the designer to navigate the future. This class is required for undergrad Design majors. Priority for this class will be given to senior Design students.
DESIGN 141: This course will introduce the basic concepts of human factors and demonstrate the importance of understanding and considering human capabilities and limits in product and system design. This will include an overview of both cognitive and physical human characteristics, methods to analyze human factors constraints, and design methods for prototyping and evaluating the usability of physical products and systems. In this course individual- and team-based design projects are used to emphasize the integration between human factors analysis and evaluation, authoring design requirements and translating these to both physical products and systems. Prerequisites: DESIGN 1, DESIGN 11, and DESIGN 121. Strongly recommended: DESIGN 172, ME102, Psych 1. It is a required class for undergrad design majors. This class is for design students only.
DESIGN 151: Business Design: Building for Impact introduces business, growth, and product concepts as tools for design, developing student capabilities critical to the development, launch, and success of new products in for-profit and impact enterprises. Functionally, students will learn to build the business model for new products, including skills such as market sizing, cost estimation, P&L modeling, and raising capital. In addition, product-market fit, growth, and product management will be explored through class visitors, case studies, and exercises. Class projects, culminating in a final Demo Day of student projects to active angel investors and entrepreneurs, will develop teamwork and effectiveness in prototyping, live presentation, written communication, and video storytelling. This course is directed towards Design majors but appropriate for all undergraduate and graduate students interested in these topics. If you are not in the Design program, instructor permission is needed for enrollment. Strongly recommended: DESIGN 121 and DESIGN 141.
DESIGN 160: A hands-on exploration of the elements and principles of design common to all the visual arts. Through a mix of theory, analysis, and practice the student will develop their ability to interpret visual content and produce effective imagery.
DESIGN 160R: This class is a required advisory class for design juniors that will guide them in exploring personal and purposeful work. In this course, students will be encouraged to clarify their personal and design values with respect to the impact they hope to make as human-centered designers. Class activities will prepare students practically for navigating their careers beyond Stanford. Outcomes will include supporting students in developing their personal body of work and launching a digital portfolio. Throughout the course, Design Formation will allow students to build community in their cohort as well as with the broader design alumni community. Time will be afforded for students to synthesize and integrate material learned in their chosen method depth classes and domain classes. Finally, this course will prepare students to leverage these insights in service of their senior year capstone project.
DESIGN 161A: Team-based project using knowledge, methodology, and skills obtained in the Product Design major. Students will form a team, identify an opportunity space of interest, and design and implement a product (digital, physical, experiential, ... ) within that opportunity space.
DESIGN 161B: Team-based project using knowledge, methodology, and skills obtained in the Product Design major. Students will form a team, identify an opportunity space of interest, and design and implement a product (digital, physical, experiential, ... ) within that opportunity space.
DESIGN 162A: An external partner-based capstone option for design majors, this course is a culminating 2-quarter long experience in the design degree. Students will work in teams on cross-disciplinary design challenges generated with community and industry partners, allowing students to immerse in real-world constraints and work alongside partner orgs at the cutting edge of research and design to make long-lasting positive impact. Projects will align with one or more of the design program's domain sphere areas: designing for health, designing for the planet, designing for social impact, and designing for biological futures. Teams will be launched with a starting challenge brief, but will be free to hone the need and solution through iterative design cycles and stakeholder feedback. This is a Cardinal Course certified by the Haas Center for Public Service.
DESIGN 162B: An external partner-based capstone option for design majors, this course is a culminating 2-quarter long experience in the design degree. Students will work in teams on cross-disciplinary design challenges generated with community and industry partners, allowing students to immerse in real-world constraints and work alongside partner orgs at the cutting edge of research and design to make long-lasting positive impact. Projects will align with one or more of the design program's domain sphere areas: designing for health, designing for the planet, designing for social impact, and designing for biological futures. Teams will be launched with a starting challenge brief, but will be free to hone the need and solution through iterative design cycles and stakeholder feedback. This is a Cardinal Course certified by the Haas Center for Public Service.
DESIGN 170: The student will learn how to use graphic design to communicate online, in person, and through printed matter. Fundamentals of visual communications will be applied to branding exercises, typographic studies, color explorations, drawing exercises, use of photography, and use of grid and layout systems. This class was formerly listed as ME 125. This course can satisfy the visual expression elective requirement for undergrad design majors.
DESIGN 172: Design Visualization offers students a unique opportunity to acquire a new (visual) language over the span of one short quarter. Imagine a process where you can close your eyes, and, after a few short weeks, leveraging established Design Principles, open them, and imagine/draw virtually anything that comes to mind. This is our pledge to you, independent of your previous sketching experience. This course melds basics with Industrial Design discipline, dividing the skillset into three parts; the ability to representationally draw in three-dimensions, exploring the nuances of form & materials, and storytelling using the juxtaposition of those forms. DESIGN172 initially focuses on the first component, building the structural foundation for perspective drawing. We then introduce basic lighting and shading theory to 'complete the picture'. Finally, we delve into storytelling and figure drawing, embracing the human element of conveying new products and services. As confidence builds, analysis gives way to individual choice. While we express & explore solutions with traditional analog medium, we often bridge 'the digital divide', expressing final projects in several media choices, introducing "sketch rendering" in AI, and stirring in portfolio & professional advice en route. NOTE: When taken in conjunction with DESIGN 173 (Digital Design Principles and Application), this pair of courses can satisfy the visual expression elective requirement for undergrad Design majors. DESIGN 172 should be taken first before enrolling in DESIGN 173.
DESIGN 173: Leveraging foundational design principles, we use analytical problem-solving approaches to facilitate digital media creation. In class, we explore these techniques in real time and engage in group-based critique and encouragement. We embrace the latest Generative AI platforms and teach designers how to maintain creative control in a rapidly evolving technological space. The curriculum covers image generation, compositional references, storyboarding, animation, and 3D model outputs. This class emphasizes strengthening students' storytelling abilities and selecting the appropriate tools to tell the tale(s). A series of diverse, rapid projects are brought together with an eye to related student project portfolio development. NOTE: When taken in conjunction with DESIGN 172 (Digital Sketching), this pair of courses can satisfy the visual expression elective requirement for undergrad Design majors. DESIGN 172 should be taken first before enrolling in DESIGN 173.
DESIGN 183N: This seminar course will explore the science behind generative AI, the likely future of tools such as DALL-E, ChatGPT, GPT-4, and Bard, and the implications for education, both in and outside of structured school environments. Students in the course will work in teams to each become experts in some aspect of AI and in some way that generative AI could create a new future for education. The background for this course is the public release of ChatGPT, which created new awareness of the potential power of AI to dramatically change our lives. In considering the possible implications for education, ChatGPT has sparked dreams of automated personal tutors, customizable teaching assistance, AI-led collaborative learning, and revolutions in assessment. In addition to optimistic projections, there are clear and significant risks. For example, will AI-assisted learning be culturally appropriate and equally available to all? Can it increase opportunity for underprivileged learners worldwide, or will it accentuate privilege and privileged views? Will it help us learn faster, or distract us from thinking deeply about difficult problems ourselves? As experienced student learners, members of the class will be able to draw on their own educational history and design learning approaches that could change the future of their education and others in college or at other stages of their lives.
DESIGN 187: The new space industry has the potential to impact and sustain life on Earth and beyond. For example, emerging space technology can shape the way we design habitats, food, and spacecraft for low-Earth orbit or the Lunar surface, as well as the products we use here on Earth. However, this requires us to take a deeper look at the potential influence on humanity and pushes us to declare our life mission as a lens for what we engineer. The aim of this IntroSem is to help undergraduate students "shoot for the moon" and "declare their mission" via an integration of curriculum from aerospace engineering and human-centered design. In this 10-week course, students will engage with some of life's hardest questions: Who are you?; Why are you here (i.e., on Earth and at Stanford)?; What do you want?; and How will you get there (i.e., Mars or your dream job after Stanford)? In addition, students will pitch new space-related, human-centered technology to potential stakeholders. To give students exposure to actual careers in aerospace design and engineering, mentors from industry will be invited to engage with students throughout the course and provide feedback on design projects. Are you go for launch?
DESIGN 191: Directed study and research for undergraduates on a subject of mutual interest to student and staff member. Student must find faculty sponsor and have approval of adviser.
DESIGN 191A: For undergraduate students. Meets the requirements for curricular practical training for students on F-1 visas. Student is responsible for arranging own internship/employment and faculty sponsorship. Register under faculty sponsor's section number. All paperwork must be completed by student and faculty sponsor, as the Student Services Office does not sponsor CPT. Students are allowed only two quarters of CPT per degree program. Course may be repeated twice.
DESIGN 192: This seminar introduces students to academic research in Design. Specifically we will look at research relating to Design in roughly three areas: Research into Design (the study of how designers, engineers, and teams design), Research for Design (tools and methods to support designers and engineers), and Research through Design (applying the design process to understand different phenomena, solutions, and interventions). Additionally, we will explore methods of conducting research in design. Students will work towards creating a research proposal and plan. This course is required for students participating in the Undergraduate Research Internship in Design, but is open by application to other students.
DESIGN 204: Slightly controversial and built with designers concerned with both great products and social impact in mind, Forbidden Design seizes the unique times we find ourselves in where products and innovations that were once deemed forbidden or even illegal are now major factors in the marketplace and spectrum of the human experience. Students will conduct industry climate analyses, social impact assessments, map the problem space, build projection based prototypes, design meaningful forums, and apply personal reflections to how they exist in their professional fields. Students will engage in tangible design education partnered with dives into the responsibility of design within the quagmires of politics + culture.
DESIGN 208: This project-based studio immerses students in a real-world climate challenge through a focused team-based design project. Student teams will apply human-centered design and systems thinking to understand stakeholder needs, navigate complex social and environmental systems, and identify opportunities for meaningful impact. Through research, synthesis, and prototyping, teams will develop and test interventions that contribute to a more sustainable and resilient future.
DESIGN 210: The course introduces students to the principles of design and thinking; major issues related to migration and cities; different forms of evidence for evaluating and responding to challenges and opportunities stemming from migration; and the application of concepts, theories, and data to design solutions. What brings people to a new place? What happens when they arrive? Who gets to decide what that community becomes? Students in this course will be introduced to major issues related to migration and cities, and to some core design abilities for taking action. A major portion of the course will center learning through real world projects with experts in the field. Students will work in teams to assess actual opportunities and challenges human migration creates, and to design real responses.n
DESIGN 223: In DESIGN 223 (formerly known as ME 248), students will design and create a silver pendant. Beginning with a basic introduction to design and CAD, students use a computer aided design tool to create a 3D model of their pendant design. Next, using machines and processes at the Product Realization Lab, students build a version of their part in a wax-like material. This part is then used in a lost-wax investment casting process to turn the printed part into a cast silver part. Finally, the students are introduced to a set of hand tools they will use to turn their cast silver part into a finished silver pendant. By application only, see course listing notes below.
DESIGN 229: Light, sound, narrative, and presence are the most powerful levers for shifting human consciousness, yet traditional design rarely teaches us how to wield them with emotional weight - or to confront the reality that you cannot change a broken system outside yourself without first interrogating the systems living inside you. This studio treats artistic creation not as static ornament, but as an active, strategic force for social transformation and radical self-examination. Pairing the accessibility of design with the uncompromising edge of fine art, you will compose soundscapes, produce short films, take the mic in live performance sessions, and stage public artistic interventions. By pushing you directly into controversy, emotional risk, and creative discomfort, this course helps you turn personal conviction into provocative public artifacts - equipping you with a multi-medium portfolio that proves creative expression can change a civilization by first changing the person making it.
DESIGN 231: What makes design different from the other "making" professions like engineering or the traditional arts? Drawing on the philosophy of the Eames and Stanford's own Bob McKim, we emphasize the centrality of "need." What is a need, and how can it shape our design work for the better? This class aims to answer those questions through a series of hands-on design research challenges, culminating in an intensive end-of-quarter team project aimed at uncovering unmet needs. Skills and themes include: observation, ethnographic interview techniques, cultural psychology, data analysis and synthesis, metaphorical frames, concept generation (brainstorming) and systems thinking. Come prepared to "dance with systems"!
DESIGN 232: The d.school is turning 20 years old this year, and we are commemorating this occasion in October, 2025 with an exhibit. This advanced studio experience will challenge students to design an immersive, highly experiential format for this event. We'll consider exhibit design, space, visual design, media design, and more. Students will collaborate with each other and d.school faculty. There is opportunity to continue work through the summer and participate in exhibit construction.
DESIGN 235: The future is already here. It's just unevenly distributed - and unevenly imagined. View from the Future is a conversation series that collapses the distance between where design is heading and where you are right now. Each week, a different practitioner. A different field. A different vantage point on what's coming - and what's already here for those paying attention. Every week in this class, you'll sit across from someone who is living at the genuine edge of their field. Their careers rarely followed a straight line. Their job titles often didn't exist before they invented them. And the skills that got them there? Not always the ones you'd expect. View from the Future is a conversation series that collapses the distance between where design is heading and where you are right now. Each week, a different practitioner. A different field. A different vantage point on what's coming - and what's already here for those paying attention. Past guests have come from architecture, AI hardware, sports media, regenerative fashion, civic journalism, healthcare innovation, luxury, and beyond. What they share isn't a field - it's a posture. They anticipate what's coming. They imagine what doesn't yet exist. They design with both in mind. By the end of this course, our students don't just know more about where the world is going. They see themselves differently within it - as active participants in shaping it, not passive recipients of whatever arrives.
DESIGN 236P: Print on Purpose is where designing forward while looking back at the legacy of print for social change meets in an immersive design space. Join us for a rigorous course that probes the intersection of visual expression and freedom of speech. We dissect the role print has played as a driver of social change, covering media ranging from newspapers, zines, posters, pamphlets, vinyl album covers, stickers, to lawn signs. Print on Purpose is an introduction to visual communications tools and processes that impact the way our work is produced and received. It's about experimentation with typography, drawing, and imagery, and inevitably rolling up your sleeves and producing prints. This course emphasizes the importance of DIY production methods and works with students to utilize the resources available to them to produce printed materials. Critiques will be a fundamental part of each project, as will the incorporation of feedback. You will be expected to participate in evaluating your own work and that of your peers in group settings.
DESIGN 236S: Bring your art and design work into the material world through this hands-on making course centered on the tools in the d.school Community Printshop. Students will learn to be engaged members of the Printshop through production methods that focus on creating work for their peers and the broader Stanford community. You will receive foundational training in letterpress and risograph printing, linoleum carving, and bookbinding. Work produced in this class will include posters, postcards, zines, and limited edition prints created via illustration, collage, digital design, and traditional plate-making methods. You will gain practical experience in operating a printshop and using Adobe Creative Suite and Spectrolite for file preparation. Letterpress instruction covers printing on platen and cylinder presses, setting and printing from metal and wood type, and using photopolymer plates. Risograph training includes printing from drawings on paper and producing multicolor images from raster and vector files.
DESIGN 237: This course explores the intertwined practices of printing and type design as both creative and communal endeavors. Students will learn the foundations of letterpress and risograph printing, gaining hands-on experience in preparing files, setting type, and producing prints ranging from posters to zines. At the same time, the course introduces the principles of type design, with an emphasis on both Latin and Global Scripts. Through workshops, critiques, and collaborative projects, students will investigate how tools, substrates, and design choices shape letterforms and printed matter alike. By the end of the quarter, students will have both practical skills in operating a community printshop and a working prototype of their own typeface, situating their work within broader conversations about visual communication and cultural expression.
DESIGN 238: This seminar is for students who are interesting in the future of sustainable mobility and to view that challenge through the historic lens of some of the world's greatest cars. Students will participate in discussions from a number of perspectives - engineering, aesthetic, historical impact, etc. to establish a set of criteria to evaluate an automobile. They will then use these to be a part of a judging team at the Pebble Beach Concours d'Elegance to decide the recipient of the Center for Automotive Research at Stanford (CARS) Award for Automotive Innovation, which is given to the car that they believe truly impacted the challenge of a sustainable future through excellence in technology and innovation. Students will have the opportunity to present the award on the lawn at Pebble Beach Lodge in August. The Pebble Beach event is the leading concours for automobiles in the United States.
DESIGN 240: Build your creative confidence and sharpen your design thinking skills with analog-architected interventions. This experiential studio engages students with fast-paced, hands-on exercises that train your intuition and expand the design context from which you operate every day. You'll develop mental, emotional and physical foundations for agency, cognitive flexibility, and a strong bias toward action - skills expert designers use across every phase of their process. You won't be sitting back and taking notes - you'll be moving, making, and failing forward in every session to grow your personal toolkit for tackling design challenges across any discipline, and in your everyday life. Published scientific research based on this course curriculum shows that performing these class activities will expand your creative capacity in statistically significant ways.
DESIGN 242: Aerogel! Kintsugi! Silkworms! In this course we'll dive head (and hands!) first into a world of "wild" and wondrous materials and processes. Through hands-on projects, you'll discover tools, materials, and mindsets beyond the traditional rapid prototyping toolkit. You'll develop material literacy and intuition by exploring materials that may be soft, living, crunchy, and/or disobedient. Together, we'll uncover both new ways of making and new ways of connecting with our material world. An application is required, but students of all levels and disciplines are encouraged to apply.
DESIGN 245: Why does finance need redesigning? Finance is something we all have to navigate yet remains complex and elusive to crack for many. It's a system that often does the opposite of design thinking: breaks down around nuance and reinforces exclusionary practices. In a world bursting with apps, products, solutions - why is this problem space still not "solved"? Why finance needs redesigning is one of the many questions we will investigate in this course. Students will explore the history of financial institutions in this country, take their design thinking skills into the field, and reimagine solutions beyond today's reality. Past years' classes have given students access to executives from Amazon Web Services, Apple, Blackrock, J.P. Morgan Chase, Munich Reinsurance, Bank of the West (now BMO), Silicon Valley Bank and Wells Fargo, the community of Paradise California, pioneering small-to-medium sized businesses founded by diverse trailblazers, and professional and student athletes seeking to manage personal finance and wealth. Recent themes for the course include financing sustainable cities and regional peace. We've found that the language of design allows us to discuss the rarely discussed challenges of finance, its impacts on families and communities, and how to shift the narrative for the better in the current and future generations.
DESIGN 248: Join us to learn the methods of co-design, the practice of designing WITH and not FOR communities. We'll explore how to identify projects well suited for co-design, how to shift from the "hero" to the "host" as designers, and how to practice cutting edge co-design methods. We'll hear from expert practitioners in the social and for-profit sectors and apply methods that pull from community organizing, change management, and social justice movements. You will become versed in the frameworks and tools of co-design, a practice that is on the forefront of the Equity Design movement. It will help to have experience with design thinking, but you do not need to be a long-time or deep practitioner. Lived experience and passion will be highly valuable.
DESIGN 255: Our world is increasingly laden with many forms of measurable data. While visualizations and data graphics abound, the effectiveness of the stories they tell relies on thoughtful design. In this hands-on course, students will experiment with and practice the fundamental (mostly analog!) skills required for telling compelling stories with qualitative and quantitative data: asking better questions, exploring the unknown, sorting and synthesizing, drawing connections, prototyping, crafting, and presenting visual data stories. Students spend over half of the quarter exploring and visualizing data about themselves: fostering inquiry, discovery, and creation of personally meaningful stories and potential portfolio pieces. This class is for all experience levels, whether you have years of experience with data visualization, or are looking to explore what's possible -- together we will learn how to navigate and create at the intersection of data, design, and self-expression. n
DESIGN 257: First we invent our technologies - and then we use our technologies to reinvent ourselves, as individuals, as communities and ultimately, as a planetary society. The result has been a vast wave of astonishing innovations that in turn have generated the profound challenges facing humanity today. You will work with a suite of forecasting methods essential to cultivating innovator's effective foresight, the ability to spot hidden trends, identify new opportunities, develop responsive innovations and anticipate unintended impacts in the face of exponential uncertainty. Our topical focus this quarter will be the Western US megadrought. We will develop an integrated forecast of its long-term trajectory, explore its implications and working as teams, translate our insights into innovation opportunities, encompassing engineering solutions, behavioral insights and policy recommendations. You will learn the basics of technology diffusion, and how to apply a variety of methodologies including scenario planning, field anomaly interaction, cross-impact analysis, expert judgment elicitation and design thinking tools.
DESIGN 259: The famous computer scientist, Alan Kay, once said, "The best way to predict the future is to invent it." As such, we are all responsible for inventing the future we hope we and our descendants will experience. In this highly interactive course, we will be exploring how to predict and invent the future and why this is important by focusing on a wide range of frontier technologies, such as robotics, AI, genomics, autonomous vehicles, blockchain, 3D Printing, VR/AR, synthetic meat, etc. The class will feature debates in which students present utopian and dystopian scenarios, and determine what has to be done to inoculate ourselves against the negative consequences. Limited enrollment. Admission by application: dschool.stanford.edu/classes.
DESIGN 261: In this course, students explore upstream systems that influence health and then apply their learning to generate ideas for making everyday life healthier on campus. Taking a systems approach to health includes the deliberate upstream design of the places we live, learn, work and play to support living in ways that keep people well - physically, emotionally, financially, and socially. Spring Quarter 2026 we are reimagining the Stanford food ecosystem, especially Stanford residential dining, in partnership with Residential & Dining Enterprises.
DESIGN 262: In Design for Healthy Behaviors, we apply Stanford's philosophy, spirit and 65-year tradition of Design Thinking through a lens of proactive health. You will work on three health-design projects with three different student partners this quarter. You will team up with a partner and work directly with a Patient-Volunteer, who is managing a complex chronic health condition, in the Patient-Volunteer Project (PVP) to help and enable them to improve elements of their health over the course of the quarter. These patients have volunteered, and been referred to our class, by one of the teachers of the course, Dr. Nancy Cuan MD, who helps to lead the Stanford Coordinated Care Program at the Stanford Hospital. There will be two 3-week long Personal Health Projects (PHP) with different partners to improve some self-chosen aspects of your own health. Through these three projects, from the teaching team, from a number of invited guests and from each other, you will learn and use the fundamentals of the Design Thinking process to develop your own process of coaching other's, and guiding your own, healthy habit formation to enable the improvement of long-term health.
DESIGN 264: The health care system is not particularly healthy nor caring, nor much of a system. What if you could help redesign healthcare and health-adjacent systems to work for all of us? In this course, students will collaborate with patients and their caregivers, many from underserved communities, to reimagine the future systems that better serve their needs. Blending co-design, digital product design, and foundational AI, you'll tackle the complex intersections of chronic illness, health policy, and social well-being to create solutions that deliver the right care, at the right time, in the right place. Working in teams alongside clinicians, community leaders, and technologists, you will design, prototype, and test concepts grounded in the real worlds of those you serve, all with the aim of making health care more just, accessible, and human.
DESIGN 265: If ever there was a space ripe with opportunity for design, it's one where intentional (mind)set and setting are critical to the quality of the user experience. Foundational design decisions are being made today that will shape how psychedelics show up in our healthcare systems and everyday lives, without strong design thought leadership in the room (yet). This class is for anyone exploring the ecosystem of psychedelic medicine, including people who wouldn't normally call themselves designers - mental health and wellness practitioners, government policymakers, venture builders, the psychedelic medicine-curious, and fierce social justice and equity advocates pushing for spiritual development through sacred plants. And for experienced designers, it's a chance to practice navigating ecosystem complexity in an emergent industry - something we're all doing right now, one way or another. This course is a creative playground spanning mental health and wellness, policy, business, technology, culture, art, nature, plant medicines, and people. You'll practice design depths like systems design, speculative design, and visual communication, while hearing from a wide range of expert voices across the ecosystem - social justice, law, clinical practice, spiritual traditions, and indigenous communities, to name a few. On a personal level, we want you to leave with a life-centered design approach: a way to mindfully navigate, design, and thrive during times of disruption and mental distress.n
DESIGN 266: Learn what it takes to build a viable AI company for the healthcare domain. This project-based course gives you a hands-on learning experience of what it's like to build an AI company that makes doctors faster, patients happier, and healthcare outcomes better. Artificial intelligence (AI) is transforming healthcare, unlocking new possibilities in diagnostics, personalized medicine, and patient care. This course explores cutting-edge AI models and techniques designed to address real-world healthcare challenges, empowering participants to develop innovative solutions for clinical teams. Using a human-centered design approach, students will develop a product by identifying user needs, prototyping, and iterating. Class projects will center on deploying AI solutions, leveraging real-world datasets and training models in collaboration with partners at Stanford Medicine. Key topics include AI-driven diagnostics, predictive analytics for patient outcomes, and intelligent workflow optimization. Through hands-on exercises, clinical mentorship, and interdisciplinary collaboration, participants will shape the future of healthcare. Guest speaker's featuring product managers and engineers from Google and Meta, successful healthcare entrepreneurs, and leading venture capitalists will share insights on innovation and investment in the healthcare AI ecosystem. Registration is by approval. To apply, complete the course application: https://forms.gle/wWHodH4s5WDsP5sy5. Selected students will receive a registration code.
DESIGN 268: In the wake of recent tensions in the electoral space, there has never been a more critical time to explore the intersection of design and election administration. This engaging, project-based course will offer students the opportunity to apply design principles to a compelling, timely design space, and work on real-world applications that can help improve how local election offices administer elections. Through exposure to multiple levels of design, including visual design, service design, strategic design, and systems design, students will gain a comprehensive understanding of how design can be applied to the administration side of elections.
DESIGN 271: Legal aid groups, government agencies, and state courts offer free help to people experiencing housing, debt, family, and other major life problems. This policy lab will examine how to make this legal help more accessible, trusted, and impactful. How can more people be aware and empowered to use legal help, especially in a more equitable way? Students in this policy lab will research and design national strategies for making legal help and government services more discoverable, user-friendly, and trustworthy. Students will conduct user research, technology experiments, and legal research to identify what specific initiatives might make legal help more engaging and impactful. The students will be able to explore a range of new kinds of innovations from technology, to community partnerships, to service design--and help justice organizations make a coherent strategy for increasing uptake and engagement with their public services. This class is open to Stanford Law students, and available for cross-registration for graduate and undergraduate students from across campus. We encourage students from outside the Law School to apply. Students will be working together in small teams. Grading will be based on presentations, written assignments, class participation, and group work. CONSENT APPLICATION: To access the consent application for this course, go to link SLS Registrar https://registrar.law.stanford.edu/ and then click SUNetID Login in the top right corner of the page. See application for deadline and instructions.
DESIGN 272: This policy lab will build on the work of the Fall 2022 policy lab that researched three specific issues related to the Dobbs decision: medical abortion, restrictions on travel, and issues related to the collection and dissemination of information between and among providers and patients. The goal of the Spring 2023 policy lab is to develop a strategy for getting the information developed in the Fall 2022 policy lab to the field. In particular, students in the policy lab will identify how service providers and funders effectively receive information (offline through community-driven programs or online through websites and working with Google search and other engines) and specifically how they are obtaining information related to state abortion laws. The students will identify and speak with relevant legal and policy organizations to determine how they share legal information with funders and service providers. This "market research" will help inform (1) who our client should be and (2) what kind of materials (offline v. online) we should develop (what forms work best, how should the information be presented and executed?) In the last few weeks of the quarter, the students will propose and develop initial drafts of those materials. Given that the terrain is rapidly changing, students will likely update the legal information collected by the Fall 2022 policy lab to ensure it remains accurate. Elements used in grading: Attendance, Class Participation, Written Assignments, Final Paper.
DESIGN 273: In this course, you will learn fundamental negotiation & design skills, and apply them to environment- and sustainability- based simulations and case studies. We will show you how, where and why design thinking adds unique efficacy to your burgeoning negotiation abilities: map and design the structure and process of a negotiation; identify the underlying motivations of the stakeholders in your negotiation scenarios; surface the distinct differences between everyday conversation and strategic negotiation; improve listening and communication; develop your gravitas and adaptability in the moment; practice teamwork in both preparation and execution of complex, multi-party negotiations. You will work through exercises that isolate these skills and then apply them in simulated negotiations, at least one in every class session, to develop and embed a confidence/competence feedback loop for your continued growth as a negotiator. This course is geared for students who are dedicated to and passionate about sustainability, environment, and social justice - from any school or discipline at Stanford, not just the Doerr School. This course requires an application and acceptance by the instructors. No previous negotiation or design thinking training is required.
DESIGN 275: This course is designed for and focused on sustainable career development for emerging professionals. Join us for an immersive 10-week experiential journey where students explore how innovation and leadership in career paths, whether you are an employee or entrepreneur - become more meaningful and sustainable when cored in alignment with personal purpose. We will excavate personal purpose through a series of activities and assignments that teach technical approaches to building a reflection praxis. The designers and instructors of this course are enthused to engage students in a course that through self-discovery, co-design methodologies, storytelling, reflection, creative exercises, and exposure to world-changing leaders, challenge students to design not only projects or ventures, but the foundations of the life they want to create. In a world shaped by globalization, rapid technological transformation, and unprecedented access to information and opportunity, students are also challenged to reflect on both the positive and complex realities of global business, including its power to create progress, economic and educational inequalities, connection, disruption, responsibility, and influence at scale. Rather than starting with "What should I build?", this class begins with a deeper question: "Why do I want to build at all?" Key themes include: Innovation and design thinking, personal narrative exploration,, leadership development, and design practices to help students co-design a future aligned with who they truly are and hope to become. Excitingly, key source materials for this class include highly popular design guides from the Stanford d.school literary offerings.
DESIGN 276: In an era of rapid technological disruption, culture design must do more than engage employees. It must work toward human flourishing as a path to sustainable transformation. In this course, we view today's business challenges as an opportunity to invent entirely new ways of working and connecting. Serving as embedded culture designers, student teams will partner directly with forward-looking organizations to tackle real-world organizational friction. You will leverage behavioral and experience design frameworks to diagnose systemic challenges, analyze how disruption alters human dynamics, and run live cultural experiments. Throughout the quarter, you will follow a rigorous discovery, design, and delivery process to prototype and implement actual culture policies, collaboration rituals, and organizational artifacts alongside your partner organizations. In doing so, you will sharpen core design abilities critical for leading modern, evolving systems: (i) Moving between abstract and concrete: Grounding high-level organizational strategies and cultural values into tangible, daily team behaviors. (ii) Experimenting rapidly: Launching and iterating low-fidelity culture prototypes to test psychological safety, adaptability, and team adoption. (iii) Communicating deliberately: Designing transparent feedback loops, alignment strategies, and communication norms that keep human teams connected amidst rapid change.
DESIGN 277: This very interactive course, including workshops, case studies, and projects, presents a scaffolding of skills that all aspiring leaders need, including how to frame and reframe problems, work with diverse stakeholders to address a challenge, and make ethical decisions that are consistent with your values. Whether you are leading a local community effort, a for-profit venture, or a global initiative, every effective leader needs the knowledge, skills, mindset, and values to bring bold ideas to fruition. This includes understanding how to develop a vision, to see problems as opportunities, and recover from inevitable failures. As part of the course, each student will apply these skills in leading in their own life and projects they are working on outside of the course. This course is jointly offered by the Design Program and Knight-Hennessy Scholars at Stanford for these communities.
DESIGN 282: Machine learning is everywhere - but where is it in your design practice? You are the next generation of creators to harness the potential of machine learning and also to understand its implications. Expect to explore and deepen your design abilities by leveraging generative AI tools while navigating the benefits and tradeoffs as you build out your AI toolbox for design. This class invites a mix of designers, data scientists, engineers, business people, and diverse professionals of all backgrounds to help create a multi-disciplinary environment for collaboration. Through a mixture of hands-on guided investigations and design projects, students will learn to design WITH machine learning and create lasting value within their human contexts and environments.
DESIGN 283Q: A historically-informed and multidisciplinary approach to designing emerging technologies like AI, the metaverse, NFTs, IOT, and the systems in which they exist to be equitable.Throughout history, innovations in science and technology, while bold and visionary, have often resulted in catastrophic consequences for Indigenuous, Black, immigrant and other historically oppressed communities, and the environment. Today's emerging technologies, which span everything from deep fakes to self-driving vehicles, have incredible capabilities, and at the same time are plagued with algorithmic bias and lack accountability. What can we learn from our precarious past that we are not learning today, but need to? This class welcomes the curious and the creative, from interdisciplinary fields including design, computer science, art, history, political science, ethics, feminist and gender studies and professionals of diverse backgrounds. Through a variety of hands-on design projects including historical excavations, speculative fiction and world building, students will learn how to create prototypes of emerging technologies and evaluate their implications on diverse communities, the environment, and our past and future selves.
DESIGN 284: Designing for Physical AI is a startup accelerator-style, human-centered design course where students create AI-enabled products that sense, interpret, and act in the physical world. Building on the course's foundation in Extended Realities, this course expands into robotics, AI glasses, AR/VR devices, responsive environments, sensor-driven objects, and other forms of embodied intelligence. As billions of dollars flow into frontier models and AI infrastructure, human-centered design is urgently needed to translate technical capability into products that genuinely improve people's lives. Students will work in multidisciplinary teams on a Physical AI design project throughout the quarter. Teams will conduct user research, frame meaningful needs, prototype functioning proof-of-concepts, and test their ideas with real people. Along the way, students will explore how AI-assisted coding, creative agents, and rapid prototyping tools change the human-centered design process itself. The class will examine responsible innovation questions around privacy, surveillance, safety, access, environmental cost, and the social implications of pervasive AI systems. Students will receive mentorship from world-class experts across design, engineering, product, research, entrepreneurship, venture capital, AI, robotics, and XR. Hardware, software, and technical support will be provided. The course will culminate in a public exhibition attended by investors, industry professionals, designers, technologists, and potential partners. No advanced technical background is required, though experience in human-centered design, AI-assisted coding, creative technology tools, or physical prototyping is highly encouraged. Group applications are encouraged. Final enrollment codes are granted after application approval and attendance in the first week. Apply using this link: https://docs.google.com/forms/d/e/1FAIpQLSeuLjKHI6Cqz_5yhsSec3YCgetrBSWzKev0MJx1H4uzSMRMuA/viewform?usp=header
DESIGN 287: During this unique moment in time, with the pandemic still looming, and racial reckoning in America, the importance and the role of play in designing experiences is an essential tool that enables us to collectively navigate ambiguity, build trust and re-imagine assorted legacy systems. In this class students will explore the playful nature of creativity to help real world project partners infuse their products and services with joy and transform their organizations to be more playful. Students will learn how the playful mind is essential to productive thinking and underlies the creativity required for the best ideas. You will also work collaboratively to ask and answer: How might play be a vehicle for wellness? How might play connect people and rebuild community? This class is for students of all experience levels, we will redefine play as we learn, and develop skills to move from the abstract to the concrete -- with meaning, goals, and principles.
DESIGN 289: Fashion is one of the largest and most impactful industries in the world. It employs, pollutes and touches human lives and planetary systems at a scale that is hard to fathom. In Redress we will explore and prototype in the spaces between fashion, sustainability and emerging (and vernacular) technologies. We will negotiate more than-human collaborations to investigate our impacts on human and more-than-human worlds. This course offers an immersive, hands-on exploration into the realm of biomaterials, where fashion not only meets the aesthetic and functional needs of people but also aligns with the principles of environmental stewardship and symbiosis with the Earth. Enrollment is by application.
DESIGN 292: In 2014, the d.school's Stanford2025 project invited the Stanford community to imagine the future on-campus experience in the face of challenges raised by online learning. This produced deep insight into fundamental student needs and values. Now, in 2026, we invite students to enroll in this course and design the future in the face of questions, risks, and potential sweeping change from AI. Design teams will imagine possible futures and plan for college-age experiences within them. We will formulate and wrestle with questions such as: How might we view consciousness, perception, values and emotion in the future? How might college-age students view their career and life trajectories, if specialized skills are widely available to all? What will people need to master and how will they learn over their expanding life course? Will love, friendship and other human relationships be very different? What could go terribly right or wrong in any or all directions? Students in the class will work in small teams and build to think, prototyping in many mediums, with AI and without. Mid-quarter you'll make short science fiction films set in various futures that are neither utopias nor dystopias, but complicated future worlds people actually live in. We will then explore what might replace current college in some of these scenarios. The quarter ends with a showcase for the Stanford community, and public artifacts built to stand on their own and influence the university's future.
DESIGN 294: Schools and learning communities are facing unprecedented challenges today. From the advancement of AI and the impact of climate change to the imperative of ensuring each child receives the necessary support in a rapidly changing world, the need to bolster educational communities has never been more critical. In this project-based course, students will foster partnerships with local and global communities, gaining the opportunity to explore and experiment with design techniques and tools. This hands-on approach allows them to co-create solutions that are contextually relevant and responsive to the needs of the communities they partner with and serve. The course offers an applied exploration of human-centered design, learning sciences, digital technologies, and education entrepreneurship. By the end of the course, students will be equipped with the skills necessary to drive meaningful change for learners in any community.
DESIGN 297: In this course we creatively apply information technologies to collectively attack Global Grand Challenges (e.g., global warming, rising healthcare costs and declining access, and ensuring quality education for all). Interdisciplinary student teams will carry out need-finding within a target domain, followed by brainstorming to propose a quarter long project. Teams will spend the rest of the quarter applying user-centered design methods to rapidly iterate through design, prototyping, and testing of their solutions. This course will interweave a weekly lecture with a weekly studio session where students apply the techniques hands-on in a small-scale, supportive environment. Note: Cardinal Course certified by the Haas Center for Public Service
DESIGN 298: A course focusing on creating small scale objects in precious metals, with equal attention given to design and the process of investment casting in the Product Realization Lab. By application only, see notes below.
DESIGN 301: Design can change the world. But whether it's for better or worse isn't a static outcome. Your work - like you - will change with time. Sometimes for the better. Sometimes for the worse. This course will introduce you to the powers and responsibilities of design work through a series of hands-on project-based learning experiences. You will explore a medley of design mindsets, methods, and mediums - but most importantly, you will have a better understanding of who you are and how you can use design to change the world, for the better. Please note: This course is designed specifically for first-year graduate design students and is not open to students outside the cohort.
DESIGN 315: How do you see yourself and your work? How do your perceptions shape your choices, creativity, and sense of agency? A course of study for students preparing to launch out of Stanford. This course is an exploration of how to lead a more intentional, creative, and committed life - one that aligns with your values, aspirations, and actions. Each week, we read and discuss a book that challenges our understanding of work, meaning, perception, and personal agency. Through structured conversations, students connect ideas across disciplines (ranging from anthropology, to fine art, to technology), exploring the nature of creativity, purpose, and self-perception. The course is experiential: Classes have activities designed to drive discussion and put concepts into action to be evaluated, students also take on two projects - one focused on removing a challenge or constraint in their life, and another open-ended project tackling something entirely new (past projects have included writing a book, starting a business, learning a skill, or making a bold change). Take this course if you are interested in inspecting and rethinking how you approach your life and work - so you can move forward with clarity and confidence. This class was conceived and taught by Bernie Roth for 40 years as Designer in Society, the current teaching team instructed with him for the past 8 years. If interested in the history please listen to the podcast: https://podcasts.apple.com/us/podcast/yellow-eyed-cats-with-bernie-roth/id1812088224. First class attendance is mandatory. Enrollment application required on the first day.
DESIGN 341: This is the second course in the Graduate Needfinding series; DESIGN231 is a pre-requisite. How do we affect change as designers within complex social systems? In order to do this, we are going to have to consider our own commitments and choose a system or set of interconnected system problems to become a "systems practitioner" within. This course builds upon a foundation of Needfinding Skills but expands into new territory by recognizing designers as change agents with internal values and commitments. By both creating space for these burgeoning designers to reflect and equipping them with the Frameworks and Tools to understand and challenge current system norms, we aim to set up our students to run new, brilliant, culturally sensitive and sustainable design interventions for systems change. Expect to be challenged, evaluate your paths of self-reflection, and both give and receive thoughtful critique.
DESIGN 360R: Advanced Reflective Practice supports students in developing as adaptive learners who are able to synthesize and integrate their experiences from across the MS Design program and beyond. Through immersive interactions and technology-enhanced asynchronous work, students strengthen their capacity to navigate open-ended problems while understanding their own learning processes. The curriculum emphasizes ethical reflection, challenging students to consider the broader implications and responsibilities of their design decisions. This class is open to MS Design students only.
DESIGN 361A: This class is the scaffold for the second year MS Design thesis project. Each second year student completes a year-long thesis. Topics are specific to each student and lie at the intersection of chosen method and domain focus areas. Prerequisite: Open only to second year MS Design students who have successfully completed the first year of coursework.
DESIGN 361B: This is a continuation of DESIGN361A. This class is the scaffold for the second year MS Design thesis project. Each second year student completes a year-long thesis. Topics are specific to each student and lie at the intersection of chosen method and domain focus areas. Prerequisite: Open only to second year MS Design students who have successfully completed the first year of coursework.
DESIGN 361C: For graduate Design students, and select students by application, who have completed DESIGN361A&B. This class is the scaffold for the second year MS Design thesis project. Each second year student completes a year-long thesis. Topics are specific to each student and lie at the intersection of chosen method and domain focus areas. Prerequisite: Open only to second year MS Design students who have successfully completed the first year of coursework.
DESIGN 365: Advanced creative studies is a studio course for advanced students to take their visual design work to a higher level. Students will work on multiple elective visual & product design projects in areas of their choosing. The class format will include presentations, critique, discussion and guidance from the faculty in an intimate setting.
DESIGN 368: Leadership Lab is a one-of-a-kind, leadership course that immerses you in real-world leadership challenges. This non-traditional course offers practical experiences not typically covered in traditional leadership classrooms. This hands-on learning experience is crucial for Stanford students who want to combine technical know-how with leadership in cross-functional teams. Throughout the quarter, students will be immersed in a range of experiences where they will be asked to apply what they are learning live. Some examples from past years: working directly with a business leadership team to implement organizational changes; learning practical leadership techniques from professional sports teams; focusing on the art of gathering and how to leverage physical space, context and analogue artifacts to guide others effectively, without formal authority; and working to articulate the core values in yourself as a leader and in your team to build a genuine sense of shared purpose. Leadership Lab is a must-take class for anyone eager to develop practical leadership skills that stick, no matter the environment. There are only 28 spots available. Submit your application by March 8, 2027 5p PST at: https://forms.gle/B4sFZxjTaN4fFvRQ9. For questions, reach out to the teaching team. Undergraduates are also encouraged to apply.
DESIGN 374A: The Creativity in Research Scholars program is a one-quarter studio experience for Stanford PhD students ready to move beyond the lab and into the world. By combining human-centered design with the latest prototyping tools for emerging technologies, this course empowers researchers to translate their academic work into impactful solutions, ventures, and career pathways. In this fast-paced, experimental studio, you'll expand the research context from which you operate every day. This program is designed for Stanford PhD students across all disciplines.
DESIGN 374B: Creativity in Research Scholars is for Stanford PhD students across all disciplines. In addition to their primary research activities, these individuals are learning and applying design thinking to push the boundaries of their work and create entirely new applications and approaches to their research. PhD students will integrate design thinking tools into their research culminating in a personal project. We will teach the students on how to employ different research mindsets and approaches to enable PhD students to explore their research in new creative ways. This program is meant for doctoral students that are eager to use creative practices and collaboration to create impact.
DESIGN 377: Curiosity Corner exposes students to a range of leadership perspectives related to the Knight-Hennessy Scholars quarterly theme. The Spring 2025 theme is "Career Paths and Decisions." In each session we host guest experts who deliver a short talk, followed by a candid, open discussion. Spring quarter guests will focus on careers in academics, government, medicine, nonprofits, large companies, startups, and venture capital. There is also a quarter-long project that involves reflecting on each session as well as overall takeaways. In person class attendance is required.
DESIGN 379: At Stanford, there's a myth that your start up idea is everything. It isn't. In fact, the odds that your initial idea succeeds are effectively zero. What separates founders who break through from those who don't is not the quality of their first idea; it's the quality of their method. How they generate many ideas. How they build fast, test ruthlessly, and iterate without ego. Launch Principles is built on that truth. At Stanford, the idea gets all the glory. In this course, we focus on what actually matters: how you do the work. Launch Principles is designed for aspiring entrepreneurs who want to develop the foundational mindset, frameworks, and skills that every founder must command before, and during, the chaos of building a business. This course stands on its own as a rigorous introduction to what it actually takes to go from zero to traction. At the heart of this course is a single, non-negotiable truth: the founder's most critical skill is the ability to experiment prolifically and learn from those experiments fast. Everything else follows from that. You'll develop that muscle through hands-on work - identifying and pressure-testing ideas, running real-world experiments, and building the judgment to know when to push forward and when to pivot. What you'll develop: (i) The ability to generate, evaluate, and validate business ideas with discipline and speed, (ii) Resilience not just tolerance for failure, but the capacity to extract insight from it, and (iii) A validated concept and a path forward. No prior experience is required. Launch Principles is open to any aspiring founder ready to do serious work on the fundamentals of entrepreneurship. Attendance at the first session is mandatory. Enrollment application required on the first day.
DESIGN 391: Directed study and research for graduates on a subject of mutual interest to student and staff member. Student must find faculty sponsor and have approval of adviser.
DESIGN 391A: For graduate students. Meets the requirements for curricular practical training for students on F-1 visas. Student is responsible for arranging own internship/employment and faculty sponsorship. Register under faculty sponsor's section number. All paperwork must be completed by student and faculty sponsor, as the Student Services Office does not sponsor CPT. Students are allowed only two quarters of CPT per degree program. Course may be repeated twice.
DESIGN 399: Most startup courses teach you to plan. Launchpad teaches you to find out. In ten weeks, you will prototype your idea and put it in front of real customers not to validate a plan, but to learn things you can't learn any other way. What you discover in the market will reshape your thinking, and conviction, more than any interview or business model canvas ever could. That cycle of building, testing, and adjusting is the core skill this course develops. The goal isn't to graduate with a finished company. It's to graduate with the tools, instincts, and conviction to keep going because all founders pivot, dramatically, in the years that follow. Branch Metrics started as a smart pet collar. Sequel started as a tampon for athletes. What Launchpad builds is the founder, not the specific business they walk in with (we know that will change). The course is staffed largely by Launchpad alumni founders who have been where you are (recently). Before applying, spend time on the alumni pages (https://www.launchpad.stanford.edu/alumni) and reach out to a few Launchpad Alumni directly. Their experience is your best honest preview of what Launchpad is. Graduate students and Seniors only. No exceptions. You must attend 2 office hours and then apply to launchpad in early March look at the website for latest information. launchpad.stanford.edu
DESIGN 809E: Want to build AI that actually matters? AI for Legal Help is a two-quarter, hands-on course where law, design, computer science, and policy students team up with legal aid organizations and court self-help centers to take on one of the biggest challenges in tech today: using AI to expand access to justice. You'll work directly with real-world partners to uncover where AI could make legal services faster, more scalable, and more effective - while ensuring it's safe, ethical, and grounded in the realities of public service. From mapping workflows to spotting opportunities, from creating benchmarks and datasets to designing AI "co-pilots" or system proposals, you'll help shape the future of AI in the justice system. Along the way, you'll learn how to evaluate whether AI is the right fit for a task, design human-AI teams that work, build privacy-forward and trustworthy systems, and navigate the policy and change-management challenges of introducing AI into high-stakes environments. By the end, your team will have produced a substantial, real-world deliverable - such as a UX research report, benchmark dataset, evaluation rubric, system design proposal, or prototype concept - giving you practical experience in public interest technology, AI system design, and leadership engagement. This is your chance to create AI that works for people, in practice, where it's needed most. CONSENT APPLICATION: To apply for this course, students must complete and submit a Consent Application Form available at SLS Registrar https://registrar.law.stanford.edu/. Cross-listed with the Law School (LAW 809E). This is a Cardinal Course certified by the Haas Center for Public Service.
